If f_omega does not depend on the last digit omega_d, the inner product can be rewritten as an average over h' in Z_N^{d-1} of the square of an inner average, hence is non-negative; in particular <(f)>_{U^d} >= 0 for d >= 1, and one defines ||f||_{U^d} := <(f)>_{U^d}^{1/2^d}. Then phi is realizable over k, i.e. isomorphic to a representation Phi -> GL_n(k). The proof: it suffices that phi be isomorphic to sigma(phi) for every k-automorphism sigma of k', because the Brauer group of a finite field is trivial so there is no Schur index; and phi and sigma(phi) have the same characteristic polynomials and are semisimple, hence isomorphic by Curtis-Reiner Thm 30.16.

label: Theorem 3.1: the average size of S_2(E) over any large family is 3, via a Tamagawa-number evaluation
excerpt: Call a family F of elliptic curves over Q defined by congruence conditions LARGE if, for all but finitely many p, Inv_p(F) contains every (I,J) in Z_p x Z_p with p^2 not dividing Delta(I,J). Then, when the curves of any large family are ordered by height, the average size of the 2-Selmer group S_2(E) is 3. The family of all elliptic curves, every family cut out by finitely many congruence conditions on the coefficients, and the family of all semistable elliptic curves are all large. The proof evaluates the average of #S_2(E) - 1 as Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R)) prod_p Vol(PGL_2(Z_p)), which equals 2 zeta(2) prod_p (1 - p^{-2}) = 2, the Tamagawa number of PGL_2 over Q.

label: Corollary 1.2: average 2-Selmer rank at most 1.5, and why this does not compute the Mordell-Weil rank
excerpt: From the exact sequence 0 -> E(Q)/2E(Q) -> S_2(E) -> Sha_E[2] -> 0 one gets r_2(S_2(E)) = r(E) + r_2(E(Q)[2]) + r_2(Sha_E[2]). Using the elementary inequality 2 r_2(S_2(E)) <= 2^{r_2(S_2(E))} = |S_2(E)| and Theorem 1.1, the mean of the left-hand side is at most 1.5, hence so is the mean of each of r(E), r_2(E(Q)[2]) and r_2(Sha_E[2]) separately. Since 0% of elliptic curves have rational 2-torsion, the mean of r_2(E(Q)[2]) is 0. Therefore the limsup of the average rank of all elliptic curves over Q, ordered by height, is at most 1.5.

label: The Legendre symbol: Euler's criterion, multiplicativity and Gauss's lemma
excerpt: Let p be an odd prime. (Theorem 2.20) Exactly half the elements of Z_p^* are squares. (Theorem 2.21, Euler's criterion) For alpha in Z_p^*, alpha^{(p-1)/2} = +-1; it is +1 if alpha is a square and -1 if not. (Theorem 12.1(i)-(iii)) Consequently (a|p) == a^{(p-1)/2} (mod p), so (-1|p) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}; the symbol is multiplicative, (a|p)(b|p) = (ab|p); and it depends only on a mod p. (Theorem 12.2, Gauss's lemma) If p does not divide a, put alpha_j := ja mod p for j = 1,...,(p-1)/2 and let n be the number of j with alpha_j > p/2; then (a|p) = (-1)^n.

label: Quadratic reciprocity and the supplementary law at 2, by the lattice-point counting proof
excerpt: (Theorem 12.3) If p is an odd prime and gcd(a,2p) = 1 then (a|p) = (-1)^t with t = sum_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2} floor(ja/p); and (2|p) = (-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}. (Theorem 12.4) If p and q are distinct odd primes then (p|q)(q|p) = (-1)^{((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2)}. Together with Theorem 12.1(i)-(iii) these give the complete Legendre-symbol calculus: the main reciprocity law, the supplementary law at -1, and the supplementary law at 2.

label: Definition 2.1: good dihedral prime
excerpt: Let Q: N -> N be defined by Q(1) = 1 and, for n >= 2, Q(n) = the largest prime dividing n. For rho-bar: G_Q -> GL_2(F_p-bar) continuous, a prime q different from p is a good dihedral prime for rho-bar if (i) rho-bar restricted to I_q is of the form diag(psi, psi^q) with psi a NON-TRIVIAL character of I_q whose order is a power of an odd prime t such that t divides q+1 and t > max(Q(N(rho-bar)/q^2), 5, p); and (ii) q is 1 mod 8, and 1 mod r for every prime r with r <= max(Q(N(rho-bar)/q^2), p). If such a q exists, rho-bar is called locally good-dihedral (for the prime q), or q-dihedral.

For a p-torsion-free complex, (η_p M)^n={x∈p^nM^n : dx∈p^{n+1}M^{n+1}} is a subcomplex of M*[p^{-1}] (Construction 2.1.3; for complexes in nonnegative degrees η_pM⊆M, footnote 1). For termwise p-torsion-free M, a Dieudonné structure F is equivalent to a map of cochain complexes α_F:M*→(η_pM)*, α_F(x)=p^nF(x) for x∈M^n, with inverse F(x)=p^{-n}α(x).

The constant is effectively computable.

label: Nerve, classifying space and its cell structure

A functor induces a cellular map, giving a faithful (not full) functor from small categories to CW complexes. There is a canonical cellular homeomorphism BC ≅ B(C^op) not induced by a functor, and B(C × C′) → BC × BC′ is a homeomorphism if one factor is a finite complex or if the product is given the compactly generated topology. label: Natural transformations give homotopies; adjoints and initial objects
excerpt: A natural transformation θ: f → g between functors C → C′ induces a homotopy BC × I → BC′ between Bf and Bg. Consequently a functor admitting a left or right adjoint is a homotopy equivalence, an equivalence of small categories is a homotopy equivalence, and a category with an initial or a final object is contractible (so every comma category C/d and d\C is contractible).

label: Π₀, π₁, coverings and local coefficient systems of BC
excerpt: π₀(BC) is the set of objects modulo the equivalence relation generated by the existence of a morphism. The category of covering spaces of BC is equivalent to the category of morphism-inverting functors C → Sets, equivalently functors C[C⁻¹] → Sets from the groupoid obtained by formally inverting all arrows; hence π₁(BC, X) is canonically the automorphism group of X in C[C⁻¹], and a local coefficient system of abelian groups on BC is a morphism-inverting functor C → Ab. For connected C and a maximal tree T, π₁(BC) is generated by symbols [f] for morphisms f modulo [t] = 1 for t ∈ T, [id] = 1 and [f][g] = [f∘g].

label: Homology of a small category and of its classifying space

For a local coefficient system L (a morphism-inverting functor), H_p(BC, L) ≅ H_p(C, L), and dually for cohomology with derived limits. For a discrete group G and G-module M this recovers group homology H_*(BG; M) = H_*(G; M), and H₁(BG; Z) = G/[G, G].

label: FS V.1.1: D_et([*/G],Lambda) is the derived category of smooth G-representations
excerpt: Let G be a locally pro-p group and Lambda a ring with n Lambda = 0 for some n prime to p. There is a natural symmetric monoidal equivalence D(G,Lambda) -> D_et([*/G],Lambda) under which the forgetful functor D(G,Lambda) -> D(Lambda) corresponds to pullback along * -> [*/G]. The same holds after base change to [Spa C/G] for any complete algebraically closed C/k, and the base-change functor D_et([*/G],Lambda) -> D_et([Spa C/G],Lambda) is an equivalence.

label: FS V.5.1: Bernstein-Zelevinsky duality on compact objects of D_et(Bun_G,Lambda)

label: FS II.2.7: an axiomatic GAGA theorem for a locally ringed spectral space with an ample twist

Then pullback along the natural map (X,O_X) -> X^alg is an equivalence between vector bundles on X^alg and on X, and H^i(X^alg, E^alg) -> H^i(X,E) is an isomorphism for all i >= 0. label: FS II.2.9: X_C^alg is connected regular noetherian of dimension 1 with PID complements
excerpt: Let C be a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field over F_q. Then X_C^alg is a connected regular noetherian scheme of Krull dimension 1; the map |X_C| -> |X_C^alg| induces a bijection between the classical points |X_C|^cl and the closed points of X_C^alg; and for any classical point x, the complement X_C^alg \ {x} is the spectrum of a principal ideal domain.

label: FS II.1.11-II.1.12 and II.1.22: classical points, maximal ideals and PID/Dedekind structure
excerpt: Let U = Spa(B,B^+) be an affinoid subset of Y_C. Then for any maximal ideal m of B the quotient B/m is a nonarchimedean field, and Spm(B) -> |U| is a bijection onto |U|^cl = |U| intersect |Y_C|^cl. U has finitely many connected components, and if U is connected then B is a principal ideal domain. Correspondingly, the classical points of X_C are |Y_C|^cl/phi^Z and are in bijection with Div^1(C); for U = Spa(B,B^+) an affinoid open of X_C with U connected, B is a Dedekind domain (in fact a PID, by the Picard computation).

label: FS II.2.17: quotients by contracting automorphisms of taut locally spectral spaces
excerpt: Let X be a taut locally spectral space such that for every x the set X_x of generalizations of x is a totally ordered chain under specialization. Let gamma be an automorphism of X whose fixed-point set X_0 is a spectral space, such that (i) for all x, gamma^n(x) converges to X_0 as n -> +infinity, and (ii) for all x outside X_0, gamma^n(x) leaves every quasicompact open as n -> -infinity. Then X_0 is closed, gamma acts freely and totally discontinuously on X minus X_0, and (X minus X_0)/gamma^Z is a spectral space.

excerpt: Call a sheaf integral if the eigenvalues of all Frobenii are algebraic integers. The weights of a mixed integral sheaf are ≥ 0: if an algebraic integer α is pure of weight n relative to q and of degree d, its norm is an ordinary integer of absolute value q^{nd/2}, so n ≥ 0. (3.3.3) For f: X → Y of finite type over Z and F integral and mixed of weights ≤ n, R^i f_! F is mixed of weights between 0 and n + i; if i exceeds the maximal fibre dimension d, the weights lie between 2(i − d) and n + i, because R^i f_! F and R^i f_! F(i − d) are integral by SGA 7 XXI (5.2.2) applied to the fibres.
